title: Overflow
summary: Overflow describes what happens when content does not fit inside its box.

subtopics.title: Main property
subtopics.explanation: `overflow: visible` lets content extend beyond the element’s box. This is the common default. It is like a sheet of paper sticking out of a too-small folder. It can be useful for shadows and menus, but nearby elements may overlap. Check that the visible content does not cover controls or create confusing reading order. For example, a code sample can scroll horizontally without widening the whole article.

subtopics.title: What it changes
subtopics.explanation: `overflow: hidden` clips content at the box edge and does not provide a user scroll control. It is like trimming the paper where it crosses the folder. This can contain decoration or crop an image, but it can also hide text and focusable controls. Never use it to conceal content that users need to reach. For example, a tooltip may need visible overflow so it is not clipped by its parent.

subtopics.title: Another useful choice
subtopics.explanation: `overflow: auto` adds scrolling when content exceeds the available box. It is like a document drawer that becomes scrollable only when full. This can help with wide code samples or a bounded message panel. Give the region a clear name when needed, and make sure keyboard users can scroll it. For example, a long table can use a bounded scroll region with a clear accessible label.

subtopics.title: Common behavior
subtopics.explanation: `overflow-x` and `overflow-y` control horizontal and vertical overflow separately. For example, a code sample may need horizontal scrolling without making the whole page wider. It is like choosing which side of a container can open. Test on touch screens, and avoid making users scroll in two directions for ordinary reading. For example, test keyboard focus inside a scroll container to ensure the focused control stays visible.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: Clipping or scrolling changes whether content remains reachable. Test with keyboard focus, browser zoom, narrow screens, and long translated text. This is like checking that every paper can still be retrieved from a storage box. If a control or label disappears, adjust the layout rather than hiding the overflow blindly. For example, avoid clipping a validation message beneath a fixed-height field wrapper.

foundations.overview: Overflow describes what happens when content is larger than the space available for it. CSS can let the extra content show, clip it, or make it scrollable. Think of a box that is too small for its papers: the papers can stick out, be cut off, or be reached by scrolling. Choose behavior that keeps important content available to mouse, keyboard, touch, and zoom users.
foundations.whyItMatters: Overflow decides what happens when content does not fit its box. Making that choice carefully prevents hidden information and gives people a way to reach long content.
foundations.browserPerspective: During layout, the browser measures the content's size against the box's size. If content is larger and overflow is non-visible, it establishes a scroll container (a scrollport) and reserves space for scrollbars where needed. Non-visible overflow also creates a Block Formatting Context, changing how floats and margins behave inside.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Scrollable sidebars and chat panes, truncating titles with ellipsis, containing floats, hiding decorative overflow on hero sections, and creating horizontally scrolling tables or carousels on mobile.
foundations.businessImpact: Clean truncation and scroll regions keep interfaces tidy across screen sizes, reducing layout bugs that frustrate users and hurt conversion on key screens.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Understanding overflow eliminates a whole class of 'why is my page scrolling sideways?' and 'why won't this text cut off?' bugs, making layouts robust to variable content.
foundations.performanceImpact: Scroll containers can be GPU-composited and are generally efficient, but very large scrollable content and frequent scroll-driven reads/writes can cause jank; keep scroll handlers light and avoid layout thrashing.
commonUseCases: Vertically scrolling sidebars and chat windows (overflow-y: auto with a max-height)
Truncating a single line of text with an ellipsis
Containing floated children by establishing a BFC (overflow: hidden)
Horizontally scrollable tables or carousels on small screens

commonMisconceptions.reality: It does nothing on its own. You also need overflow: hidden and white-space: nowrap on the same element.

commonMisconceptions.myth: overflow: auto always shows a scrollbar.
commonMisconceptions.reality: auto shows scrollbars only when content actually overflows; scroll always shows them.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Setting overflow has no other side effects.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Any non-visible overflow value creates a Block Formatting Context, which contains floats and stops margin collapsing across the boundary.
It can clip text, focus rings, and controls that users need to see or reach.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Auto overflow creates the same experience on every device.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Scrollbar and touch behavior vary, so test the actual interaction on supported devices.

visualExplorer.title: How overflow handles oversized content
visualExplorer.caption: Step through each overflow value to see whether content spills, clips, or scrolls.

steps.title: The problem
steps.description: A fixed-size box has content taller than itself. By default the content spills outside the box (overflow: visible).

steps.title: overflow: hidden
steps.description: The overflow is clipped and hidden. No scrollbar appears, and the hidden content is unreachable by the user.

steps.title: overflow: scroll
steps.description: Scrollbars are always shown, even when content fits — giving a consistent gutter but sometimes empty scrollbars.

steps.title: overflow: auto
steps.description: Scrollbars appear only when content overflows. This is the usual choice for scroll containers.

steps.title: Per-axis control
steps.description: overflow-x and overflow-y let you scroll one direction and clip or show the other independently.

interactiveExamples.title: A scrollable box
interactiveExamples.explanation: A constrained height plus overflow-y: auto turns the box into a vertical scroll container.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A bordered box about 140px tall with a vertical scrollbar revealing the extra paragraphs.

interactiveExamples.title: Truncate with ellipsis
interactiveExamples.explanation: overflow: hidden + white-space: nowrap + text-overflow: ellipsis cuts a long single line with '...'.

files.index.html: This is a very long title that will not fit on one line and gets cut off

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A 240px box showing the start of the title followed by an ellipsis where it overflows.

interactiveExamples.title: Containing floats with a BFC
interactiveExamples.explanation: A parent with floated children collapses to zero height; overflow: hidden establishes a BFC so the parent wraps them.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The bordered parent wraps around both floated boxes instead of collapsing to a thin line.

hints: A scroll container needs a size constraint like max-height before it can overflow.
overflow-y: auto adds a vertical scrollbar only when needed; overflow-x: hidden blocks sideways scrolling.

keyTakeaways: `overflow: visible` lets content extend beyond the element’s box.
`overflow: hidden` clips content at the box edge and does not provide a user scroll control.
`overflow: auto` adds scrolling when content exceeds the available box.
`overflow-x` and `overflow-y` control horizontal and vertical overflow separately.
Clipping or scrolling changes whether content remains reachable.
